newsitem.title: USA: Emerging mkts may not see post-FOMC relief rally.
newsitem.headline: Emerging mkts may not see post-FOMC relief rally.

text.p: Emerging markets debt may not get a "relief rally" if the U.S. Federal Reserve does what the markets expect and raise short-term interest rates by 25 basis points, U.S. analysts and traders said.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has prepared the market for a preemptive strike against inflation, and by all accounts, U.S. Treasury securities have priced in a 25-basis-point rise in the U.S. overnight bank lending, or federal funds rate.

Traders said they expected that once the rate hike becomes official, a "relief rally" could put emerging market bonds back on a winning streak. But that scenario appeared to be receding on the eve of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

Echoing the opinion of many analysts, Raul Elizalde, senior quantitative analyst at ING Barings, said emerging markets would scrutinize signs of inflation to prepare for another rate increase at the FOMC meeting on May 20.

"It's going to be a non-event," he said, referring to the possible rate hike on Tuesday, adding that emerging market bond traders may not follow the path of selling in anticipation and buying on the fact.

Tulio Vera, emerging markets debt strategist at Bear, Stearns and Co Inc, did not rule out a fleeting positive tone in the Treasury market, which, in turn, may lend some support to emerging market bonds. But the rally could prove to be inconsequential, he predicted.
In spread terms, emerging markets debt probably would not challenge the tightness in February at least through the second quarter, he said.

Although emerging markets debt has lost about five to six percent in the current market correction, compared with a decline of 12 percent during February and March of last year, Vera said the outlook now is far less bullish.
"The whole rally was predicated on global liqudity," he said. "There are many variables to consider."
Besides U.S. rates, investors are nervously watching the timetable for European Monetary Union, which has underpinned the performance of European high yield bonds, Vera said.
Traders said they hope spread volatility calms down after the expected rate hike becomes official, noting that uncertainty has driven many marginal players out of the market.
"It is not just a 25-basis-point rise in the cost of money," said a Brady bond trader. "It depends on how fast the Fed would push up rates."
In the second half of last year, yields on 30-year U.S. Treasury were slowing rising, but spreads to Brady bonds were trending tighter, he noted.
If the market perceives that a second preemptive hike won't be coming soon, high yield seekers will return, the trader said.
But Elizalde noted that volatility in emerging markets debt has risen sharply since February with no sign of subsiding.

Historical volatility measured by the daily return of J.P. Morgan's Emerging Market Bond Index plus (EMBI+), over 10-day intervals, rose from about 6.0 percent in February to 14 percent in March, he said.
In view of the continuing turbulence, Elizalde said he expected spreads to trade in a 100-basis point range over the next two months.
"We are inclined to buy bottom and sell top, rather than initiate new positions," he said.
